issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a male civilian-in-war-zone trauma profile, sexual objectification as a central trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it lacks support from memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other items consistently describe war-related threat, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory trauma memory rather than sexualized threat, making this trigger hard to integrate into the same trauma presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding as a trigger is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items. No memory, threat, or appraisal items reference water, drowning, environmental disaster, or any related theme. Given the otherwise interpersonal/war-threat profile, this trigger appears disconnected from the formulation.

issues.item: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the indexed trauma type. For a civilian in a war zone, water/flooding and alcohol smell are hard to reconcile with the threat, memory, and appraisal items unless there is some specific unreported trauma context linking them. The rest of the profile centers on generalized danger, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory recall, but these two triggers imply a different situational pattern that is not otherwise represented.

The maladaptive strategy set is partly disconnected from the rest of the formulation. Drug use is plausible as a broad coping strategy, but excessive exercise and concealing clothing suggest body-focused avoidance or managing visibility/safety in a specific way that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items presented. Given the strong Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies and Threat → Maladaptive Strategies links, these strategies should plausibly follow from the reported triggers and threat beliefs, but these two items do not clearly do so.

vignette:
Rohan is a 24-year-old South Asian man who works as a junior diplomat, currently stationed in Washington D.C. following a posting abroad that ended abruptly under circumstances that have since reorganised the entire architecture of his inner life. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 66, and he arrives at the intake appointment dressed in a loose, long-sleeved shirt despite the warmth of the season, sitting with his back to the wall and his eyes tracking the door at intervals throughout the session.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Rohan was stationed at a diplomatic mission in a city that came under sustained military assault over the course of several days. He had been attending a formal reception at a colleague's residence when the first strikes landed several blocks away. The building shook. Glasses fell. And then, in the minutes that followed, a portion of the outer wall collapsed under secondary pressure, and Rohan found himself on the floor amid smoke, plaster dust, and the smell of burning - a dense, particulate odour that mixed with the spilled wine and spirits from the overturned table beside him. A man he did not recognise stumbled toward him through the debris, face bloodied, arms outstretched, and Rohan, unable to move, lay still until colleagues reached him. He was not gravely physically injured. That fact, he has since decided, is evidence of something damning about him rather than something fortunate.

In the weeks that followed evacuation, Rohan began to notice that certain things undid him without warning. The smell of alcohol - at a dinner, near a bar, even hand sanitiser with the wrong chemical note - would return him without transition to the floor of that residence, the dust in his throat, the man walking toward him. A car backfiring, a door slamming in an adjacent room, construction work three streets over: any sharp, percussive sound could produce the same violent displacement, the same certainty that it was happening again, that the walls were coming down. He found himself in those moments not remembering the event but inhabiting it, speaking from inside it, and then returning to the present disoriented and ashamed. What frightened him most in these episodes was not the fear itself but his inability to accept reassurance. When his partner, Priya, held him and told him he was safe, he could hear the words and find them meaningless - not because he doubted her sincerity, but because he had come to believe that safety was simply not a category that applied to him anymore.

He began to manage. He started running - long distances, at punishing hours, pushing past discomfort into exhaustion, then further. He began using cannabis most evenings, and occasionally something stronger when the nights were bad. He took to wearing long, layered clothing whenever he left the apartment, operating on the quiet logic that if he was not visible, he was less of a target. He stopped attending diplomatic receptions entirely, citing workload, and then stopped attending most social functions associated with his posting. His supervisor has noted his withdrawal in two informal conversations, and a formal performance review is pending. Priya has told him she feels she is losing him, and he has not known what to say, in part because he knows what happened but finds that when he tries to speak about it the words simply do not exist - there is the event, vivid and sensory and present, but no language that reaches it. He can sometimes smell the smoke and spilled spirits when he sits with the memory, but he cannot explain to anyone, including himself, what he experienced.

What has settled most heavily over these fourteen months is not any single symptom but a set of convictions that have quietly taken up residence. He is certain there is something about him - some quality he cannot name - that made him a person to whom this would happen. He has lost whatever faith he held in the coherence of the world and in the people who move through it. Strangers who approach him in ordinary situations - a colleague crossing a room, a server leaning over to take his order - produce a spike of alarm that he finds humiliating and cannot override. He does not believe the future contains much for him. It was Priya who finally said the word therapy aloud, and it was the look on her face when she said it that brought him here. What he is most afraid of is that nothing will change. What he is most hoping, tentatively and almost against his will, is that someone can help him find the words.
